prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The winner of the 82nd annual Scripps National Spelling Bee said Friday she is "pretty excited" but a little tired. Kavya Shivashankar of Olathe, Kansas, reacts to winning the Scripps National Spelling Bee on Thursday night. "This has been my dream for so long; I've always wanted to win the bee," Kavya Shivashankar, 13, of Olathe, Kansas, told CNN. "I was just really excited when I was able to go up and spell the last word." The eighth-grader won $40,000 in cash and prizes for nailing the final word, "Laodicean," which means lukewarm or indifferent, particularly in matters of politics or religion. This year's bee -- an event that has skyrocketed in popularity thanks to exposure on television and in movies -- started Tuesday in Washington with a record 293 spellers. Kavya endured 15 rounds. In an event that has seen contestants crack under the strain of the national spotlight, Kavya -- competing in her fourth national finals -- appeared composed throughout.  Watch the poised winner describe the thrill » . As she spelled words such as "phoresy," "hydrargyrum" and "huisache," she calmly went through the routine of asking each word's pronunciation, origin and roots before ticking their spellings off for the judges. "I focus so much on my word; I don't really pay attention to all the cameras and photographers and all the media in front of me," she said Friday. Kavya's father, who is her spelling coach, would tap his foot in time as she spelled the words, and at one point he appeared so confident that he waved to someone while his daughter was in the middle of spelling a word. Second-place finisher Tim Ruiter of Reston, Virginia, bowed out after misspelling "Maecenas," meaning a generous patron of the arts. Kavya said she would miss competing in the spelling bee, as the rules do not permit her to enter next year. "It was such a big part of my life, and I love doing it," she said. However, she may someday have a new role in the competition. "If my [little] sister gets to D.C. sometime soon, I'd really love to help and coach her," she said. Kavya attends California Trail Junior High School in the Kansas City suburb. Her hobbies include swimming, cycling and traditional Indian dance, according to the contest's Web site. She plans on becoming a neurosurgeon. The first National Spelling Bee took place in 1925, with five contestants. CNN's Devon Sayers contributed to this report.

### CNN and The E.W. Scripps Company in the Changing News Landscape

CNN and The E.W. Scripps Company are prominent names in American media. CNN is internationally recognized for its 24-hour television coverage, breaking news reporting, political analysis, and extensive digital presence. Since its launch in 1980, the network has played a major role in shaping continuous news broadcasting.

The E.W. Scripps Company has a broader portfolio that includes local television stations, national media brands, and digital platforms. Through Scripps News, the company has sought to provide accessible, fact-based national reporting while drawing on the resources of its local newsrooms.

Although CNN and Scripps operate with different structures and audiences, both face similar challenges. Viewers increasingly consume news through websites, mobile applications, streaming services, and social media rather than traditional television. As a result, the two organizations continue to adapt their distribution strategies and explore new ways to engage audiences.

CNN’s global reach and Scripps’ strong local presence illustrate two important approaches to modern journalism. Their ability to maintain public trust, invest in original reporting, and respond to changing technology will help determine their roles in the future of news.

*By Staff Writer*  
**WASHINGTON, May 28, 2009** — After four years of increasingly close finishes, 13-year-old Kavya Shivashankar finally captured the championship she had pursued through thousands of hours of study, winning the 82nd annual Scripps National Spelling Bee by correctly spelling “Laodicean.”

Kavya, an eighth-grader from Olathe, Kansas, calmly worked through the word—meaning lukewarm or indifferent, especially in religion or politics—before reciting its letters: “L-a-o-d-i-c-e-a-n.”

When head judge Mary Brooks declared her the champion, confetti fell onto the stage at the Grand Hyatt Washington, and Kavya covered her face with her hands. She then lifted the championship trophy as her parents and younger sister joined her.

“I can’t believe it,” Kavya said after the victory. “It’s just so amazing.”

The title came in her fourth and final year of eligibility. Kavya had steadily advanced through the national ranks, tying for 10th place in 2006, finishing eighth in 2007 and taking fourth in 2008.

“I’ve been waiting for this moment for a long time,” she said.

### A decisive final round

Kavya won after the remaining challenger, 12-year-old Tim Ruiter of Centreville, Virginia, stumbled on “maecenas,” a word for a generous patron of literature or the arts. Under the bee’s rules, Kavya first had to spell a word correctly after his error and then successfully complete a separate championship word.

She handled both, finishing with “Laodicean” shortly after 10 p.m. Eastern time in a nationally televised final on ABC.

Kavya was known on the spelling circuit for her methodical approach. Before giving an answer, she often asked for a word’s definition, language of origin, alternate pronunciations and use in a sentence. At times, she traced letters with a finger on her palm, mentally testing possible spellings before speaking into the microphone.

Her preparation was similarly systematic. With help from her father, Mirle Shivashankar, she studied word lists, roots and language patterns for years. The family’s effort turned the competition into a shared undertaking, but Kavya said the final responsibility remained hers once she stepped before the judges.

“I was nervous, but I had confidence in myself,” she said.

### Record field of young spellers

The 2009 competition began with a record 293 contestants from across the United States and several other countries and territories. Entrants qualified through local and regional bees, surviving school, community and sponsor-level contests before reaching Washington.

The field was gradually reduced through written tests and oral spelling rounds. By Thursday evening, only 11 finalists remained under the television lights.

Contestants faced words drawn from an array of languages and academic fields. In addition to familiar English vocabulary, the bee regularly tests words with roots in Greek, Latin, French, German, Italian, Spanish and other languages. Success therefore depends not only on memorization but also on recognizing pronunciation patterns, etymologies and rules governing how sounds are represented in different linguistic traditions.

The championship made Kavya the latest in a notable run of Indian American winners, reflecting the growing prominence of Indian American families and community spelling programs in the competition.

### Long history of the bee

The National Spelling Bee was founded in 1925 by *The Louisville Courier-Journal*. The E.W. Scripps Company assumed sponsorship in 1941. The event was not held for three years during World War II, making the 2009 contest the 82nd annual bee despite its 1920s origins.

The competition is open to students who have not passed beyond the eighth grade and who meet age and previous-participation requirements. Regional sponsors send their champions to Washington, where contestants take part in several days of preliminary and championship rounds.

The bee’s official pronouncer in 2009 was Jacques Bailly, a University of Vermont classics professor who won the national title himself in 1980. Bailly supplied pronunciations, definitions, sentence examples and language origins when contestants requested them, while a panel of judges ruled on each spelling.

As champion, Kavya received a $30,000 cash prize from Scripps, along with additional awards and reference materials from other sponsors. Her total winnings were valued at more than $40,000.

For Kavya, however, the trophy carried special significance. The 2009 bee was her last chance: As an eighth-grader, she would no longer be eligible to compete the following year.

Her earlier appearances had ended within sight of the title, making Thursday’s victory both a breakthrough and the conclusion of a long campaign.

“It’s a dream come true,” she said.
